ta-l1d10q1-d1e3501.summary: A divisio textus for Lombard's treatment of the Holy Spirit's procession from both Father and Son. Having treated the Son's generation, Lombard treats first the Spirit's eternal procession and then (Dist. 14 onward) his temporal procession. The eternal procession is treated in its mode (Dist. 10), its principle (Dist. 11, that the Spirit is from Father and Son), and its difference from generation (Dist. 13, why the Spirit, proceeding from the Father's substance, is not called born). Distinction 10 shows that the Spirit proceeds as love and concludes his proper name, 'Holy Spirit', a name that in a way fits Father and Son in common. It argues from Scripture, appropriating 'God is love' (1 John 4:16) to the Spirit, explaining appropriation by examples of words used both generally and properly, and noting that the Word is plainly called God's wisdom, and then from the saints. Five articles are announced: whether the Spirit proceeds as love; whether he is the love of Father for Son and conversely; whether he is the bond or union of Father and Son; whether his procession makes 'Holy Spirit' his proper name; and the number of persons.
claims: The Spirit's eternal procession is treated as to mode, principle, and difference from generation.
The Spirit proceeds as love and is therefore properly named 'Holy Spirit'.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3541.summary: First objection that the Spirit does not proceed as love. The Spirit proceeds as a self-subsistent person, but 'love' signifies not something subsistent but an inhering form or passion.
claims: Love signifies an inhering form or passion, not a subsistent.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3544.summary: Second objection. Nature is communicated only through an act of nature, and love is an act of will, not of nature. Since the whole divine nature is communicated to the Spirit in his procession, he does not proceed as love.
claims: Nature is communicated only through an act of nature.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3547.summary: Third objection. Creatures and divine persons do not proceed in the same way, and creatures proceed from God by an act of will, whose work is creation (Damascene). So no divine person proceeds by way of love, an act of will.
claims: Creatures proceed from God by will.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3551.summary: Fourth objection. The mode of a person's procession is proper to that person, since procession distinguishes the persons, but love is common to the three, as Lombard says.
claims: Love is common to all three persons.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3554.summary: Fifth objection. What is appropriated is not what is proper, being taken after the pattern of the proper, as wisdom, appropriated to the Son, is proper to no person. Love is appropriated to the Spirit, so proceeding as love is not his proper mode.
claims: The appropriated is not the proper.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3557.summary: Sed contra. The created image in the soul represents the Trinity, and in it something proceeds by way of knowledge and something by way of love. Since in the uncreated Trinity the Son proceeds by way of knowledge, another person proceeds by way of love.
claims: In the image, knowledge and love proceed, mirroring Son and Spirit.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3560.summary: Second sed contra. Knowledge is not perfect unless will is joined to it. Word is to love as intellect is to will, so the word is not perfect without love. God's Word is perfect, so a perfect love is associated with it, the Holy Spirit.
claims: Perfect knowledge requires the accompaniment of love.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3563.summary: Thomas's determination. In the procession of creatures two things are to be considered on the Creator's side: his nature, from whose fullness every creaturely perfection is produced and modelled, and his will, from whose liberality, not natural necessity, everything is given to creatures. Supposing by faith the procession of divine persons in unity of essence, for which no sufficient proof is found, the perfect procession of the persons must be the reason and cause of the procession of creatures. As the procession of creatures imperfectly representing the divine nature is traced back to the perfect image, the Son, as principle, exemplar, and reason of the quasi-natural procession of creatures, so the procession of creatures from the liberality of the divine will must be traced back to one principle that is the reason of all liberal giving. This is love, under whose aspect everything is given by the will. So there must be a person in God proceeding by way of love, the Holy Spirit. Hence some philosophers made love the principle of all nature.
claims: The procession of persons is the reason and cause of the procession of creatures.
As the Son is the exemplar of creatures' natural procession, the Spirit as love is the reason of their free, liberal procession.
There must be a divine person proceeding as love.
concepts: procession of persons as cause of creation

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3566.summary: Reply to the first objection. Love as such does not mean something perfect and subsistent, but as God's love, from which all imperfection is removed, it is something perfect and subsistent; the same holds for the word.
claims: Divine love, unlike creaturely love, is perfect and subsistent.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3570.summary: Reply to the second objection. As the first procession of nature communicates the whole divine nature, being perfect, so the first procession of will, the reason of every voluntary procession from God, communicates the whole will. In God will and nature are the same. The whole infinite will can exist only in an infinite nature and only for an infinite good, the object equal to an infinite will, so love, the reason of the will, can only be infinite. So nature must be communicated too. Love as such does not imply communication of nature, but as God's love and the first procession of the divine will it does.
claims: The first procession of the divine will communicates the whole will and therefore the whole nature, since will and nature are identical in God.
Divine love is infinite and so implies communication of the infinite nature.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3573.summary: Reply to the third objection. A creature proceeds from the will as a thing produced through the will, but the Spirit proceeds as the reason of every work of the will, just as the Son is produced as the art of everything constituted by the divine intellect.
claims: The Spirit proceeds as the reason of all voluntary works, as the Son as the art of all things made by the intellect.
concepts: Spirit as ratio of voluntary works

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3576.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. 'Love' is taken in God in three ways. Essentially, it implies no real procession or relation, only a conceptual one, as when God is called understanding and understood. Personally, it implies a real procession and relation and signifies the proceeding person itself. Notionally, it signifies the very ground of a person's procession, since love is not only what proceeds but the aspect under which other things proceed. Essential love is common to the three and appropriated to the Spirit ('God is love'). Personal love is proper to the Spirit, who proceeds as love. Notional love is a relation or notion common to Father and Son, also called common spiration, and is what 'love' means in 'the Father and Son love each other by the Holy Spirit'.
claims: 'Love' in God is essential (common, appropriated), personal (proper to the Spirit), or notional (common spiration of Father and Son).
The Spirit proceeds as love in the personal sense.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3582.summary: Reply to the fifth objection. Love, taken as proper, is not appropriated. Wisdom is appropriated in such a way that it can never be proper, because it is signified not as something going out from another but as resting in a subject, and so it is always essential and never personal. Love is signified by way of going out, while still signifying something absolute. That going out can be understood as real or as merely conceptual. As signifying something absolute, love is essential, and the implied going out is only conceptual, as in 'the same is the same as itself'. When the going out is signified as real, love signifies the personal love.
claims: Wisdom, signified as resting, is always essential; love, signified as going out, can be essential or personal.
Love is personal when its going out is taken as a real procession.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3594.summary: First objection that the Spirit is not the love of the Father for the Son or conversely. Whatever proceeds tending into another does not proceed as self-subsistent, and the Spirit proceeds as a self-subsistent person, so he does not proceed into the Son.
claims: What proceeds into another is not self-subsistent.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3597.summary: Second objection. What proceeds into something is received in it unless the recipient is defective, and there is no defect in the Son. So if the Spirit proceeds from the Father into the Son, the Son receives the Spirit. Whatever the Son receives from the Father he receives by generation, so this procession would be generation or included in it.
claims: Whatever the Son receives from the Father, he receives by generation.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3600.summary: Third objection. The Son receives from the Father, but the Father receives nothing from the Son. What something is 'into' has the character of a recipient, so the Spirit cannot be the love of the Son for the Father.
claims: The Father receives nothing from the Son.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3604.summary: Sed contra. All love proceeds from lover to beloved, and the Spirit is love. Since the Father loves the Son and conversely, the Spirit is the love of Father for Son and conversely.
claims: Love proceeds from lover into beloved.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3607.summary: Second sed contra from Jerome's authority cited in Lombard's text.
claims: Jerome supports the Spirit as mutual love.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3610.summary: Thomas's determination. In the Spirit's procession there are two things, the procession itself and its mode. Because the Spirit proceeds as a distinct, self-existent thing, he has from his procession as such not that he is from Father into Son but that he is self-subsistent. Considering the mode, since he proceeds as love, and in our understanding the beloved is that in which love terminates and the lover that from which it goes out, he can be called the love of the Father for the Son, since the Father loves the Son, and the love of the Son for the Father, since the Son loves the Father.
claims: From his procession as such the Spirit is self-subsistent; from its mode, as love, he is the mutual love of Father and Son.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3613.summary: Reply to the first objection. The Spirit is love of one person for another not because he is a proceeding person but because he proceeds as love.
claims: Being love of one for another follows the mode of procession, not procession as such.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3616.summary: Reply to the second objection. Saying the Son is loved by the Father does not predicate that the Son really receives something from the Father, only that the act of love terminates in him. So the Spirit's being the Father's love for the Son belongs not to generation but to the Spirit's procession.
claims: Being loved implies termination of love, not real reception.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3619.summary: Reply to the third objection. As 'the Father has love for himself' signifies no real termination or reception, only one in mode of signifying, so calling the Spirit the Son's love for the Father does not mean the Father receives anything, only that in mode of signifying the Son's love terminates in him as beloved.
claims: The Son's love terminating in the Father implies no reception by the Father.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3632.summary: First objection that the Spirit is not the bond (nexus) or union of Father and Son. What is distinct from certain things is not what unites them, and the Spirit is distinct from Father and Son.
claims: What is distinct from things does not unite them.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3635.summary: Second objection. A bond is a kind of mean between what it joins, but the Spirit is not the middle but the third person in the Trinity.
claims: A bond is a middle term.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3638.summary: Third objection. A bond is that by which things are joined, effectively or formally, and so it has the character of a principle. The Spirit is in no way the principle of Father and Son but the reverse.
claims: Whatever joins things is in some way their principle.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3642.summary: Sed contra from Dionysius: whether we speak of divine, angelic, intellectual, animal, or natural love, we take it as a unitive and binding power. The Spirit is the love of Father and Son, so he is their union.
claims: Love is a unitive and binding power.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3648.summary: Second sed contra from Ephesians 4:3, 'keeping the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace', so love has the character of a bond and nexus.
claims: Scripture speaks of the unity of the Spirit as a bond.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3654.summary: Thomas's determination. Love always implies the lover's delight in the beloved. When one delights in something, one draws oneself to it and joins oneself to it as much as possible, so that it becomes one's own. So love has the character of uniting lover and beloved, and since the Spirit proceeds as love, he is by his mode of procession the union of Father and Son. Father and Son can be considered as agreeing in essence, and then they are united in essence, or as distinct persons, and then they are united by the harmony of love. Even if, per impossibile, they were not one in essence, a union of love would have to be understood in them for perfect joy.
claims: Love unites lover and beloved through delight.
The Spirit, by his mode of procession as love, is the union of Father and Son as distinct persons.
Father and Son are one in essence and united as persons by love.
concepts: union by essence vs. by love

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3657.summary: Reply to the first objection. From his procession as such, the Spirit proceeds as a person; from its mode, he is the bond or union of lover and beloved. Whether Father and Son love each other by the Holy Spirit is treated in Distinction 32.
claims: Procession makes the Spirit a person; its mode makes him a bond.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3660.summary: Reply to the second objection. Insofar as he proceeds from two, the Spirit is the third person; by his mode of proceeding, he is the union of both.
claims: Being third and being the bond are compatible.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3663.summary: Reply to the third objection. Father and Son are said to be united by the Spirit not effectively but quasi-formally. Form is of two kinds. One remains and rests in what it informs, and in this way the divine essence relates to the persons, and they are united formally by essential love. Another unites formally not as inhering but as proceeding from both of the things united, as if two bodies were united by something proceeding from them, and in this way Father and Son are united by the Spirit. So it does not follow that he is their principle; rather the reverse. More in Distinction 32.
claims: The Spirit unites Father and Son quasi-formally as proceeding from both, not as their principle.
The essence unites the persons as an inhering form; the Spirit as a proceeding one.
concepts: Spirit not principle of Father and Son

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3675.summary: First objection that the person proceeding as love is not properly called 'Holy Spirit'. What is common to the three becomes proper only with something proper added. 'Spirit' fits all three ('God is spirit', John 4:24), and 'holy' is also common.
claims: 'Spirit' and 'holy' are both common to the three persons.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3681.summary: Second objection. Persons are distinguished by relations of origin, which follow the processions in our understanding, so each person should be named from some procession. 'Holy Spirit' expresses no procession or mode of procession.
claims: Persons should be named from their processions.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3684.summary: Anticipates the reply that the Spirit is so called because he proceeds as love, after the image of two lovers who 'conspire' in a kiss with mingled breath. Then 'spirit' would be taken from the likeness of bodily breath, and such names are said of God metaphorically, not properly or primarily. Personal names are found in God properly and prior to creatures (Eph. 3:15), so no divine person should be named 'Holy Spirit' in this way.
claims: Names from bodily likeness are metaphorical; personal names in God are proper and prior.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3691.summary: Third objection. The procession by way of nature is as holy as the procession by way of love, and the Son is not called 'holy son', so the Spirit should not be called 'holy spirit'.
claims: Both processions are equally holy.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3694.summary: Sed contra: all of Scripture and the whole usage of the Church name the third person this way.
claims: Scripture and Church usage name the third person 'Holy Spirit'.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3697.summary: Thomas's determination. 'Spirit' is a name imposed to signify subtlety of nature and is said of bodily and incorporeal things alike. Air is called spirit for its subtlety, and from this come 'inspiration', 'respiration', wind, and the subtlest vapours by which the soul's powers spread through the body; incorporeal things are called spirits for their subtlety, as God, angel, and soul. So two people who love each other and agree are said to be of one spirit or 'conspiring', as of one heart and one soul (Ethics 9: friends are one soul in two bodies). Subtlety means removal from materiality, and since removal from matter is greater in incorporeal things and greatest in God, spirituality by the meaning of the name is found first in God, though by its imposition it belongs more to bodies, whose subtlety is more evident to us who impose names. 'Spirit' as naming subtlety of nature is common to the three, but the Holy Spirit is named from spirituality for two reasons. The chief one, Thomas believes, is that through him and his gifts we are drawn into participation in divine spirituality as we are removed from temporal things, which is why those who despise temporal things are called spiritual. This fits him as proceeding as love, which has the character of the first gift in which all gifts are given. The other is that he is the love of Father and Son by which they love each other, and lover and beloved are said to be united in spirit.
claims: 'Spirit' signifies subtlety of nature, removal from matter, and so belongs first to God by signification.
The third person is named 'Holy Spirit' chiefly because through him and his gifts we are drawn into divine spirituality, as love is the first gift.
He is also so named as the love by which Father and Son are united in spirit.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3703.summary: Reply to the first objection. 'Holy Spirit' can be considered by the force of its words, in which case it fits the whole Trinity, or by the Church's imposition, by which it was imposed to signify one person, as a circumlocution standing for one name because of the poverty of our words, which fall short of speaking of God. In this sense it properly fits the Holy Spirit. Augustine gives the reason in Lombard's text: since he is the communion of Father and Son, it is fitting that he be named by a common name.
claims: 'Holy Spirit' is common by the force of its words but proper by ecclesial imposition.
As the communion of Father and Son, the Spirit is fittingly named by a common name.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3706.summary: Reply to the second objection. By the character of his procession the Spirit proceeds as love, and as love he is fittingly named by spirituality. So the name 'Holy Spirit' does in a way express a mode of procession, that of love.
claims: 'Holy Spirit' indirectly expresses procession by way of love.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3709.summary: Reply to the third argument. 'Spirit' is said of divine things before bodily things, so the objection fails, and Thomas does not believe the Spirit is named from that likeness of mingled breath.
claims: 'Spirit' is said primarily of God, not by metaphor from breath.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3713.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. According to Dionysius, holiness is purity free from all uncleanness, perfect and immaculate. So holiness is fittingly joined to spirituality, which also implies separation from materiality: spirituality signifies separation from matter, holiness from material defects. Alternatively, nature always acts in the same way, so in nature's work there is no right and not-right, as there is in the will's work. Holiness, which implies rectitude of will, is therefore fittingly joined to the procession of love and not to generation, which is a work of nature.
claims: Holiness, implying rectitude of will, fits the procession of love rather than generation, a work of nature.
Spirituality signifies separation from matter; holiness, from material defects.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3728.summary: First argument that there are more than three persons. In God will and nature are no further apart than intellect is. Since the person proceeding by way of will or love differs from the one proceeding by way of nature or generation, there should be another proceeding by way of intellect.
claims: Intellect is as distinct from nature as will is.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3731.summary: Second argument. The Father loves the Spirit as he loves the Son, and the love by which he loves the Son is a person, so the love by which he loves the Spirit is a person too, and there are more than three.
claims: Each love of one person for another would be a further person.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3734.summary: Third argument. The Spirit has perfect goodness and liberality as Father and Son do. The Father communicates his nature to another because of supreme goodness and liberality, the good being self-diffusive, so the Spirit will communicate his nature perfectly too. He does not do so perfectly to creatures, so he does so to another divine person.
claims: Supreme goodness requires perfect self-communication.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3738.summary: Fourth argument. God has many attributes besides nature and will, each with the character of a principle. Processions correspond to nature and will as principles, so other processions would correspond to the other attributes, and the persons would be many more than three.
claims: Each attribute with the character of principle would ground a procession.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3741.summary: Contrary argument, that there are only two persons. Persons are distinguished only by relations of origin, a relation of origin is that by which one is from another, so there seems to be one person who is from another and one from whom another is.
claims: A relation of origin has only two terms.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3744.summary: Thomas's determination: there are only three persons in God. Because of the essence's simplicity, distinction in God can only be by relation, and only by relation of origin (Dist. 26). A relation of origin cannot constitute a person if it signifies in general; it must signify something proper and determinate, since it functions as the person's constitutive difference. And since 'person' is a name of dignity, the relation must pertain to dignity. Three conditions are thus required: relation of origin, proper, and pertaining to dignity. Relation of origin in general covers two: 'one who is from another' and 'one from whom another is'. 'From whom another is' pertains to dignity but is common, so it must be specified by a special mode of origin. In God there are only two modes of origin, corresponding to the division of agents into natural and voluntary: generation by way of nature and spiration by way of will, the causes and exemplars of creaturely action. So 'from whom another is by generation' and 'from whom another is by spiration' are specified. These do not conflict, since one can be principle of several in different ways, so they constitute not two persons but one, since only what has some opposition can distinguish. This is the Father, from whom one is by generation and one by spiration. 'One who is from another' implies a relation of origin but is not enough to constitute a person, both because it is common and because it implies no dignity (one can be from another nobly or ignobly). It must be specified by a mode pertaining to dignity, and there are only two in God: 'from another by generation' and 'from another by spiration'. These cannot belong to one subject, since a thing has only one mode of origin from another, just as the same species is not from nature and from art, or from putrefaction and from seed. So one person is from another by generation, the Son, and another by spiration, the Holy Spirit. Since these relations cannot be multiplied numerically while remaining one in species, there being no material division, there are only three persons.
claims: Divine persons are constituted only by relations of origin that are proper and pertain to dignity.
There are only two modes of origin in God, generation by nature and spiration by will.
Active generation and active spiration, not being opposed, constitute one person, the Father.
Being from another by generation and by spiration cannot coincide, so they constitute two persons, Son and Spirit.
Hence there are exactly three persons.
concepts: nature and will as modes of origin

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3747.summary: Reply to the first argument. The processions of intellect and of nature resemble each other in a way that distinguishes them from procession by will. What proceeds by way of nature proceeds from one, if that one is perfect, and so does what proceeds by way of intellect, since several people do not have numerically one conception. So both modes are attributed to the Son, who is from one alone, the Father: he proceeds by way of nature as Son and by way of intellect as Word. The will tends into another and allows reciprocity, so that from two there proceeds one conformity of will, the union of both. So proceeding by way of will fits the Spirit, who proceeds from two and unites them as distinct persons. As one essence they are united by the essence, and in that respect there is essential love between them.
claims: Procession by intellect and by nature both belong to the Son, since both proceed from one.
Procession by will, which can be reciprocal, belongs to the Spirit, who proceeds from two and unites them.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3750.summary: Reply to the second argument. Even in lower beings a power does not reach its object and its own act by different acts: by the same act the intellect understands and understands that it understands. Likewise, since the Spirit proceeds as the love by which the Father loves the Son, there need not be another love by which he loves that love, especially since such a love would differ only numerically, not in concept, and such diversity cannot exist in God (Dist. 9).
claims: The same love by which the Father loves the Son extends to the Spirit; no further love-person is needed.
Merely numerical diversity cannot exist in God.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3753.summary: Reply to the third argument. Liberality and goodness are essential, and essential attributes are principles of notional acts only insofar as the essence is really the same as the property or notion. So goodness or liberality in the Father is the principle of generation only as his goodness is his paternity; in the Son goodness is not paternity but filiation. By the same goodness and liberality the Father begets and the Son is begotten, the Father spirates and the Spirit is spirated. As Augustine says, 'from whom' is a question of origin, not equality; 'of what kind' and 'how great' concern equality. So the Spirit's not producing another person does not mean less liberality or goodness.
claims: Essential attributes are principles of notional acts only as identical with a personal property.
The Spirit's not producing another person implies no lesser goodness, since origin is not a matter of equality.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3760.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. All the divine attributes are principles of production as efficient exemplar causes, as all goods imitate goodness and all beings the essence. All such procession is by way of nature, so no further modes of procession are needed in God.
claims: Other attributes are principles only of exemplary production, which is by way of nature.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3763.summary: The reply to the last argument, for only two persons, is evident from the body of the article.

ta-l1d10q1-d1e3772.summary: An expositio textus. (1) 'The Holy Spirit is the love, or charity, or dilection of Father and Son': the three terms are related by addition. Love (amor) is the simple inclination of affection toward the beloved, which in the sensitive part is a passion and is found even in irrational animals. Dilection (dilectio) presupposes choice (electio), as the name shows, and so belongs only to rational beings. Charity (caritas) adds a vehemence of dilection, holding the beloved at an inestimable price, as costly things are called dear (cara). (2) Whether he is called the unity, holiness, or charity of both, it is clear that he is not one of the two by which both are joined: he is called unity as the bond of Father and Son, and holiness as proceeding by procession of will, in which all holiness consists.
claims: Amor, dilectio, and caritas are related by addition: inclination, choice, and inestimable esteem.
The Spirit is called unity as bond and holiness as proceeding by will.

ta-l1d10q1-Dd1e3496.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 10 maps Lombard's treatment of the Holy Spirit's procession (eternal and temporal; mode, principle, and difference from generation). It places Distinction 10 as showing, through appropriation of 'God is love', that the Spirit proceeds as love and is properly named Holy Spirit, and it announces five articles.

ta-l1d10q1-Dd1e3533.summary: Article 1 asks whether the Spirit proceeds as love. Thomas argues that the perfect procession of persons is the reason of the procession of creatures. As the Son is the exemplar of creatures' natural procession, so the free, liberal procession of creatures from the divine will must be traced to a principle that is the reason of all giving, love, and so a person proceeds as love, the Holy Spirit. The replies note that divine love is subsistent and that the first procession of will communicates the whole nature, since will and nature are identical. The Spirit proceeds as the reason of voluntary works, as the Son as the art of intellectual works. Love in God is essential (common and appropriated), personal (proper to the Spirit), or notional (common spiration). Unlike wisdom, love signifies a going out and so can be personal.
claims: The Holy Spirit proceeds as love, the reason of all God's free giving.
Love in God is essential, personal, or notional; the Spirit is personal love.
The procession of persons is the cause and reason of the procession of creatures.

ta-l1d10q1-Dd1e3586.summary: Article 2 asks whether the Spirit is the love of Father for Son and of Son for Father. Thomas distinguishes procession as such, by which the Spirit is a self-subsistent person, from its mode, by which, proceeding as love from lover to beloved, he is the mutual love of Father and Son. Being loved implies termination of love, not real reception, so the Son receives nothing by it beyond generation and the Father receives nothing from the Son.
claims: The Spirit is the mutual love of Father and Son by his mode of procession.

ta-l1d10q1-Dd1e3624.summary: Article 3 asks whether the Spirit is the bond (nexus) of Father and Son. Since love unites lover and beloved through delight, the Spirit, proceeding as love, is the union of Father and Son as distinct persons, while they are one in essence. He is the third person by proceeding from two and the bond by his mode of procession. He unites them quasi-formally, as a form proceeding from both rather than inhering, so he is not their principle.
claims: The Spirit is the bond of Father and Son as distinct persons, uniting them as a proceeding form.

ta-l1d10q1-Dd1e3667.summary: Article 4 asks whether the person proceeding as love is properly called 'Holy Spirit'. 'Spirit' signifies subtlety, removal from matter, and so belongs first to God by signification, though imposed from bodies. The third person is named Holy Spirit chiefly because through him, the first gift, we are drawn into divine spirituality, and secondarily because he is the love uniting Father and Son in spirit. The name is common by the force of its words but proper by the Church's imposition, fitting him as the communion of the two, and it indirectly expresses procession by love. 'Holy' fits the procession of will, which involves rectitude, rather than generation, a work of nature.
claims: 'Holy Spirit' is properly the name of the third person by ecclesial imposition and fittingness.

ta-l1d10q1-Dd1e3720.summary: Article 5 asks how many persons there are. Thomas holds that there are exactly three. Persons are constituted only by relations of origin that are proper and pertain to dignity. There are only two modes of origin, generation (nature) and spiration (will). 'From whom another is' by each mode can coincide in one person, the Father, since the two are not opposed, while 'from another' by generation and by spiration cannot, since a thing has one mode of origin. So Son and Spirit are distinct, and relations cannot be multiplied numerically. The replies assign both nature and intellect to the Son, as proceeding from one, and will to the Spirit, as proceeding from two and uniting them. They deny any further love-person, note that the Spirit's not producing another person implies no lesser goodness, and treat other attributes as only exemplary principles.
claims: There are exactly three divine persons.
Persons are constituted by proper, dignified relations of origin through generation and spiration.
The Son proceeds by nature and as Word; the Spirit proceeds by will from two.

claims: Amor, dilectio, and caritas are related by addition.

ta-l1d10q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 10 treats the eternal procession of the Holy Spirit as love. Article 1 argues that as the Son is the exemplar of creatures' natural procession, so the free procession of creatures from God's will must be grounded in a person proceeding as love. It distinguishes essential, personal, and notional love. Article 2 holds that by his mode of procession the Spirit is the mutual love of Father and Son. Article 3 holds that he is their bond, uniting them as distinct persons quasi-formally, as proceeding from both. Article 4 explains the proper name 'Holy Spirit': 'spirit' signifies freedom from matter, through the Spirit as first gift we are drawn into divine spirituality, and holiness implies the rectitude proper to will. Article 5 shows that there are exactly three persons. Persons are constituted by proper, dignified relations of origin, and the two modes of origin, generation and spiration, yield one unoriginate principle, the Father, and two distinct proceeding persons. The Expositio distinguishes amor, dilectio, and caritas.
claims: The Holy Spirit proceeds as love, grounding God's free giving to creatures.
The Spirit is the mutual love and bond of Father and Son.
'Holy Spirit' is his proper name because through him we are drawn into divine spirituality.
There are exactly three persons, constituted by relations of origin through generation and spiration.
